clue.text: Put out bin at front — one of two

indicators.note: Whatever is at front stands ahead of everything else, so only the letter in that leading position is taken.

parts.note: the letter standing at the front of this word, which is all the clue asks for
when there are two of something, the one that is not this one is the other

explanation.surface: Somebody putting the bin out at the front of the house, one of the pair they keep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' sits inside the bin-day picture and means inconvenienced instead, which is why it never reads as a separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To BOTHER someone is to put them out — to trouble or inconvenience them, as in 'don't put yourself out'.

clue.text: Date after chemistry and kinky sex

indicators.note: After puts a piece behind the one named beside it, so the date ends up following rather than leading.

parts.note: the chemistry between two people is the bond they have
a date in history is an age, a stretch of time rather than an evening out

explanation.surface: A date arranged after a chemistry lesson, and something racier later on.
explanation.walkthrough: Two ordinary nouns are asked for in their least ordinary senses: the chemistry is the kind two people have, not the subject on the timetable.
explanation.definitionFit: BONDAGE is the tying-up practice, so 'kinky sex' points at the fetish sense rather than the word's older meaning of servitude.

clue.text: Watch money deposited in bank

indicators.note: To deposit something in a place is to leave it inside, so the money finishes up within the other word rather than beside it.

parts.note: a bank of seats or of screens is a tier, things ranged in rows
m is the standing short form for money in wordplay

explanation.surface: Somebody keeps an eye on cash being paid into a bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' is not the building the surface builds but a bank of things ranged in rows, which is the only reading that lets money be put inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A TIMER is the kitchen or stopwatch device that measures time, and 'Watch' is the noun for a thing that keeps time.

clue.text: Blow up balloon

definitions.meaning: the photographer's phrase for printing an image bigger than the negative
used as a verb, not a noun: to balloon is to swell outwards

explanation.surface: Inflating a balloon at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are verbs, and with no indicator anywhere the only clue to where the seam falls is that the sentence is three words long.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Blow up' is the photographic sense of making bigger, and to 'balloon' is to swell out — both are ENLARGE as a verb.

clue.text: Main house where one might get depressed

parts.note: the key issue is the main one, the word doing duty as an adjective
a pad is slang for the place somebody lives

explanation.surface: A grand main house that leaves its visitors gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depressed' is mechanical rather than emotional: a key is depressed when a finger pushes it down, and the definition only works on that sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A KEYPAD is the little block of keys on a phone or a door lock, and each of those keys is depressed when it is pressed.

clue.text: Semi-naked couple cuddle

indicators.note: Naked means with the outer covering taken off, so the word loses the letters wrapped round its outside.

parts.note: strip the letters off each end of this word and its middle pair is what is left standing
a brace is a pair — a brace of pheasants is two of them

explanation.surface: A half-dressed pair having a cuddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Semi-naked' looks like one adjective describing the couple, and it is really a noun with an instruction hyphenated onto it.
explanation.definitionFit: To EMBRACE someone is to hold them in your arms, the physical hug rather than the 'embrace an idea' sense.

clue.text: Over in beer garden at the back knocking back port wine

indicators.note: the over letter is placed in the middle of the beer word

parts.note: a pint is a measure of beer
O is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for an over

indicators.note: the rear of garden means only its last letter is used

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken

indicators.note: knocking back a drink, read here as turning the port's name backwards

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port

explanation.surface: Someone in a pub garden downs a glass of port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts O inside PINT to make PINOT; 'at the back' takes the N that ends 'garden'; 'knocking back' looks like drinking but turns RIO into OIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinot noir is a red grape variety and the red wine made from it.

clue.text: Love letter's opening written in bold

indicators.note: An opening is the way in at the start of something, so the letter the word begins on is what is handed over.

parts.note: a bold person is daring, and these six letters take the insertion

indicators.note: To write something in is to put it inside what is already on the page, not alongside it.

parts.note: the first letter of the word letter, cut off because the clue asks for its opening

explanation.surface: The first line of a love letter set in bold type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' is not the emotion but the way you address somebody, and the surface glues it to 'letter' so that it never looks detachable.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Love' as a form of address — calling somebody love — is exactly what DARLING is, an endearment rather than the feeling.

clue.text: Large bottom: cut showing cheek

indicators.note: A cut version of anything is shorter than the original, so the word arrives with its final letter gone.

parts.note: the backside, in the everyday British word for it
somebody showing cheek is pert, and it is this word that gets shortened

explanation.surface: A big backside, sliced, and somebody being cheeky about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large' as an adjective wants a noun attached — a bumper crop, a bumper harvest — so it reads as part of the picture rather than as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: BUMPER means unusually large or plentiful, the adjective used of a bumper crop or a bumper edition.

clue.text: Perhaps, Labour on holding a poll, finally Andy Burnham is running

indicators.note: running as in liquid or loose, so the letters are rearranged
only the final letter of poll is used

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political report: Labour, with Andy Burnham standing, holds a vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes the L from 'poll'; 'running' rearranges A, L and ANDY BURNHAM IS. 'Labour' is work and a 'holding' is a farm; 'Perhaps' marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Animal husbandry is the farming of livestock, one kind of work done on an agricultural holding.

clue.text: Person sparking up pressing a lighter

indicators.note: To press something in is to push it into place inside, so the single letter is forced between the others.

parts.note: somebody who sets a thing alight is a firer, and this word takes the insertion
the single letter that gets pushed in

explanation.surface: Somebody lighting a cigarette and pressing down on a lighter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lighter' is the comparative of light, not the thing in your pocket that makes the flame, and the little word 'a' is fodder rather than grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: FAIRER is what fair hair or fair skin becomes in comparison, fair here meaning pale, which is the sense 'lighter' carries.

clue.text: Insect transported via straight banana

indicators.note: To be transported via something is to travel by way of it, which here means passing right through its middle.

parts.note: plain speaking is straight speaking, honest and direct
the crossword's standard insect, three letters and always at work

explanation.surface: An insect hitching a ride on a straight banana.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straight' is the sense used of talk rather than of lines, and 'banana' defines by family without the 'perhaps' a setter often adds.
explanation.definitionFit: A PLANTAIN is the starchy cooking banana of the tropics, so 'banana' defines it by naming the kind of fruit it is.

clue.text: M&S restricting space to show clothing range

indicators.note: Restricting something hems it in from both sides, so the space is caught between the two letters.

parts.note: the two initials of the high-street chain, the ampersand between them contributing nothing
in printing an en is a space one letter wide
to wear an expression is to show it

explanation.surface: Marks & Spencer squeezing its floor space to display a clothing line.
explanation.walkthrough: M&S is Marks & Spencer, the British high-street chain, and 'space' is the printer's measure rather than room on a shop floor.
explanation.definitionFit: MENSWEAR is the department or line of clothes made for men, which is what a 'clothing range' names.

clue.text: Bird to cuddle bachelor in bed?

parts.note: to spoon is to lie curled up against somebody, an old word for cuddling
b is the standing short form for bachelor
somebody kept in bed is ill

explanation.surface: A bird curled up beside an unmarried man in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In bed' is a definition rather than an instruction about where anything goes, and the question mark marks the jump from lying in bed to being unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: The SPOONBILL is a white wading bird named for the flat spoon-shaped beak it sweeps through water, so 'Bird' names its class.

clue.text: Stop speaking English — virtually nothing

definitions.note: The definition is an order — 'stop speaking!' — where the answer is a single exclamation, so the two agree as things you shout rather than as parts of speech.

indicators.note: Virtually means not quite all the way there, so the word turns up one letter short of complete.

parts.note: e is the usual single letter for English
nought is nothing, zero, and it is this word that comes up short

explanation.surface: An order to stop talking English, with almost nothing said.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash is doing the setter's work, separating an exclamation from the two pieces that build it while the whole line still reads as one snapped sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Shouted on its own, ENOUGH tells somebody to stop speaking — the interjection, not the quantifier meaning sufficient.

clue.text: Have sex with old females in sack

parts.note: to lay somebody is the coarse verb for going to bed with them
o is the standing short form for old
f is female, doubled because the clue asks for more than one

explanation.surface: Bedding older women inside a sack.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain getting 'the sack' is being dismissed from a job, and the hyphen in the enumeration is the only sign the answer comes in two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A LAY-OFF is a dismissal from a job, and 'sack' is the informal British word for exactly that.

clue.text: Pair regularly on bender, ultimately they pick up debt

definitions.note: Arrears is one of those nouns that only lives in the plural — money owed is always arrears — so a singular 'debt' cannot agree with it and does not have to.

indicators.note: Regularly means at an even spacing, so letters are taken every other one instead of all of them.
Ultimately means last of all, so the closing letter of the word beside it is the whole contribution.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the word, taken at even spacing
the last letter of bendeR
ears are what pick sounds up

explanation.surface: Two people out on a drinking spree overhear something at the end of the night.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'bender' is British for a long drinking session, and the pair of drinkers hides the fact that 'Pair' is a word to be sampled rather than a description of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Payments you have failed to make pile up as ARREARS, the standing term for money overdue on a rent or a loan.

clue.text: Wash face with this soft soap

definitions.meaning: the small square cloth kept by a British basin, what an American would call a washcloth
soft soap is flattery laid on to get round somebody, and the same word is the verb for talking it

explanation.surface: Washing your face with a mild bar of soap.
explanation.walkthrough: The cloth on the basin and the waffle you talk when you are covering for something are one word, and 'soft soap' keeps the bathroom picture going while it changes sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A FLANNEL is the cloth Britons wash their face with, and to flannel is to soft-soap — flattering or waffling your way out of trouble.

clue.text: Supporter on seat in stand getting behind defender

indicators.note: Getting behind something is taking up position at its rear, so this piece follows rather than leads.

parts.note: in football a defender is a back — full-back, centre-back, wing-back
a stand is a thing something else sits on, and a rest is the same object under another name

explanation.surface: A fan in his seat in the stadium roaring on a defender.
explanation.walkthrough: The stadium keeps both wordplay words in disguise: 'stand' is a piece of furniture and 'defender' a position on the pitch, neither of them part of the crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A BACKREST is the part of a chair that holds your back up, so 'Supporter on seat' describes it by the job it does.

clue.text: British PM doesn't finish campaign

indicators.note: Something that does not finish stops before its end, so the name is written without its last letter.

parts.note: b is the usual single letter for British
Clement Attlee, the Labour prime minister who beat Churchill in 1945 and founded the National Health Service

explanation.surface: A British prime minister giving up before his campaign is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'British PM' reads as one phrase and is two separate instructions, which is what keeps the surname out of sight — nothing in the clue says a name is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A BATTLE is a sustained fight for something — a battle against illness, a battle for votes — which is what a campaign is.

clue.text: Sympathise as Charlie not off jobseeker's allowance

parts.note: Charlie is C in the radio alphabet, alongside Alpha and Bravo
a switch that is not off is on
the dole is the British name for unemployment benefit, drawn week by week

explanation.surface: Charlie is still signing on for his jobseeker's allowance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not off' is a whole piece on its own, an instruction-shaped phrase that turns out to be a plain synonym — the trick setters use for the two-letter words.
explanation.definitionFit: To CONDOLE with somebody is to express sympathy for their loss, the verb that survives today mostly inside the noun 'condolences'.

clue.text: Bird bath with rook pinching top spot off family member

indicators.note: the rook grabs the rest of the relative, so the two pieces are joined side by side

parts.note: Bath is a spa town, and a spa is a bathing place
R is the chess notation for a rook

indicators.note: the top letter of the word is taken off, as the clue is a down entry

parts.note: a crow is a member of the crow family, as the rook is

explanation.surface: A rook at the bird bath bullies a relative out of the best place.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'family member' is a corvid: the rook's relative CROW, and 'top spot off' drops its first letter C to leave ROW, which the rook R is 'pinching'.
explanation.definitionFit: The sparrow is a small brown songbird, common in gardens.

clue.text: Handle of shortened rifle concealed by jacket from tracksuit

indicators.note: the rifled letters are hidden inside the jacket letters, which wrap them
a jacket is an outer layer, so the outside letters of tracksuit are taken

parts.note: the word whose first and last letters are taken

indicators.note: the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to rifle a place is to ransack it

explanation.surface: A sawn-off rifle is smuggled inside a tracksuit top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rifle' is the verb meaning ransack; 'shortened' cuts it to RANSAC, and 'jacket from' gives TT, the outside of tracksuit, which RANSAC is 'concealed by'.
explanation.definitionFit: To handle a deal or business is to transact it, a synonym in the commercial sense.

clue.text: Get lost taking on run in country

indicators.note: Taking something on is receiving it into yourself, so the letter is admitted inside rather than added at the end.

parts.note: 'no way' is the flat refusal you give somebody you want rid of
r is the cricket scorer's mark for a run

explanation.surface: A runner out in the countryside takes on a route and goes astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get lost' is the brush-off — what you snap at somebody you want rid of — rather than the wandering the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: NORWAY is the Scandinavian country, so 'country' defines it by naming the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Admires topless chests

indicators.note: Topless means with nothing on top, and the top of a word in a down entry is its first letter, which is the one that goes.

parts.note: crates are chests, the wooden boxes things get packed in

explanation.surface: Somebody admires a row of bare chests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chests' are packing boxes rather than bodies, and 'topless' is an instruction dressed up as part of the same picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To RATE somebody is to think highly of them — 'I rate her' is the informal British way of saying you admire her.

clue.text: Botched tattoo line, briefly — nearly balls up in this drawing

indicators.note: A botched job has come out wrong, and letters that come out wrong are letters standing in the wrong order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters taken as they stand
the word line cut short, its final letter dropped before the shuffle
anagram fodder, six more letters straight off the page

explanation.surface: A badly done tattoo of a line, and balls that almost go wrong in a picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls up' reads as a phrase for a mess and belongs to the definition, where the balls are the numbered ones that come up when the draw is made.
explanation.definitionFit: The NATIONAL LOTTERY is Britain's state-licensed prize draw, and its numbered balls genuinely do come up in the drawing.

clue.text: Only fish by lake close to jetty

parts.note: a sole is the flatfish served in every seaside restaurant
l is the map-maker's short form for lake

indicators.note: The close of a word is where it ends, so this hands over the single letter jetty finishes on.

parts.note: the last letter of jettY

explanation.surface: Fishing beside a lake near the end of the jetty.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here announces itself as an instruction: 'close to jetty' reads as a position on the water and is the only piece of machinery in the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: SOLELY means exclusively, done by one thing and nothing else, which is the adverb sense of 'Only'.

clue.text: Make out while retired women swing

parts.note: to make something out is to see it

indicators.note: having retired, the word goes back, so it is read in reverse

parts.note: as can mean while, as in 'as I was leaving'

explanation.surface: A couple kiss while some retired women dance or sway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make out' suggests kissing but means see; 'retired' turns AS into SA.
explanation.definitionFit: A seesaw is a playground plank that tips up and down, so it swings back and forth.
